subtopic: NAVIGABLE WATERS PROTECTION ACT
NAVIGABLE WATERS PROTECTION ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR REMOVAL OF VESSEL CAUSING POLLUTION
speechtext:
that Bill C-39, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act (prevention of water pollution), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe a minor error has arisen, although perhaps we should deal with it later, when we find out whether there are more speakers on the bill than there is time available. I do not think that the committee on Health and Welfare is the right committee to which to send the bill. It should more properly be sent to the transport Committee, but perhaps we could rectify this error later. In any event, my Bill C-39 would amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act and insert after clause 15, a provision which would make it possible for the minister to order the owner of a vessel

which has gone aground and is causing pollution to remove the wreck or to have it destroyed, and to order that the owner of the vessel or cargo pay the full costs of such actions. Section 16 of the act as it now reads permits this to be done only in the case where the wreck in question is obstructing navigation. The purpose of this amendment is to enlarge the minister's scope so that the same powers will be granted to him to permit the removal of wrecks or other vessels when they become a danger from the point of view of pollution.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
This matter has a fairly lengthy history. It first came to my attention when a vessel of the Holland American line, sailing out of Rotterdam, grounded and eventually sank off the west coast of Vancouver Island on January 3
1968.	This vessel was the MS Schiedyk. It had on board 150 tons of heavy diesel fuel, 120 tons of light diesel oil, and a certain amount of lubricating oil. The payment of the cost of cleaning up the pollution damage that resulted from this wreck was by the government of Canada; in other words, the taxpayers of Canada. The purpose of the amendment to the act I am proposing would be to shift that burden of cost from the government and taxpayer to the people who should be responsible, namely the vessel owners as well as the people who own the cargo of that vessel.
Hon. members will recall that in the Canada Shipping Act amendments, which were considered a little over a year ago, the government attempted to introduce a provision similar to this. Those amendments were in Bill S-23, which came before the Senate in
1969.	The particular clause in that government measure which would have had the effect of my amendment to the Navigable Waters Protection Act was clause 24, which was unfortunately struck out by the Senate committee on transport and subsequently by the Senate itself. The Senate did this after hearing representations from shipping interests, the International Chamber of Shipping and other such bodies and their Canadian equivalents. The debates, which are most interesting and which I recommend to hon. members, are in the Senate proceedings of the committee on transport and communications Nos. 6, 7 and 8 of February 27, March 6 and March 13 of 1969.
It was decided by the Senators that as the provisions of clause 24 of Bill S-23 would cause Canadian law to be somewhat out of line with the legislation of other states, it
June 9, 1970

should not be passed until the international organization which concerns itself with such matters, namely, the International Maritime Consultative Organization, dealt with the matter at their meeting in Brussels in November of 1969. The meeting was held, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) represented Canada. He made a statement at this meeting in which he put forward Canada's view, and the line of argument which is behind both my amendment today as well as clause 24 of Bill S-23 of last year.
Unfortunately, at the meeting of the International Maritime Consultative Organisation in Brussels there were many states represented, some of which have no coastline but large oil interests, and some of which have coastlines but also have extensive shipping interests. Naturally, these states are less concerned about oil pollution at sea than we are. The results of pollution coming from a tanker was absolutely liable, regardless of fault, for the Canadian position that the vessel owners as well as the cargo owners should be made not accepted by the majority of states there. Some progress was made at that conference, but I think it is clear that the Canadian view did not get very far at the meeting. Let me discuss for a moment why we did not succeed. The arguments put forward, which are contained, by the way, in the Senate references which I have given the House, suggested that the nature of marine insurance would make it impossible to apply unlimited liability upon a shipping company. This argument was put forward at length. It is one that I have considered and that I reject. I would be very surprised indeed if the insurance business, which is a flexible business-we have all heard that Lloyds will insure anything- cannot find some way of insuring vessels at sea for the ultimate consequences of any shipwreck or disaster at sea. I am quite sure that if the industry put its mind to it, there is a way of insuring vessels regardless of the limit of liability. Certainly, in the case of commercial aircraft the liability of the insurer is almost unlimited. One instance which I was given showed that $80 million was paid by Insurance Companies for one airline disaster. If they can find it possible to insure a single aircraft for up to $80 million, I think it is incredible that they should argue they can only insure a ship up to a total upper limit of $10 million to $15 million.
So, I reject their argument because I think if we insist upon the idea first of a limitation and second of liability only in case of fault, we will make it quite impossible for the inno-

Navigable Waters Protection Act cent people who may have marinas, fishing camps, or who may be commercial fishermen, all those people who live along the shore and gain their livelihood from the sea, to collect from these large oil interests. Thus they will suffer from the disasters rather than the people who I think should be responsible for the costs, namely the shipping and oil companies.
It was suggested that perhaps a voluntary organization of shipping interests might be the best way to deal with the problem. It was mentioned to the committee and elsewhere that the Tanker Owners Voluntary Agreement Concerning Liability for Oil Pollution would satisfactorily take care of this particular matter. I think that the existence of such an organization does not make such legislation as I propose unnecessary. In my opinion, it is quite essential for us to have absolute liability, and to have it without necessarily requiring proof of fault on the major oil carriers.
The argument was put forward that ultimately the consumer will have to pay for any increase in cost, if the cost of shipping oil is increased and that this is bad. I submit that the consumer of oil is precisely the one who should pay, not the taxpayer, not the general public, not the people who happen to live along waterways which are frequented by these enormous vessels, but the people who use the oil. If the insurance is going to be expensive for such carriage of oil, well, that is tough; and if it increases the cost of oil, that is tough, too. However, why should the people who use that oil not bear that cost and risk? I say the people who use that oil, but naturally the company will pay in the first instance, and then will pass on the cost to the consumer. But why should the general public be responsible for the clean up, and why should little people be subjected to disaster simply because of this legal difficulty which oil companies and shipping interests see?
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
There is a second point which is most important here, and which is especially important to Canada's northland. If we continue with our present way of placing the risks on others than the oil companies and others than the consumer, we distort the costs of shipping by sea as opposed to shipping by pipe line. I think hon. members can appreciate the point, that if we allow the taxpayer to bear the cost of cleaning up oil pollution and do not put the cost where it should be, on the shipper or oil company, then we have created
June 9, 1970

Navigable Waters Protection Act a subsidy, a sort of hidden extra benefit for the oil company that intends to ship by sea. The pipeline, which perhaps might be an alternate and better method of transporting oil is not given this, subsidy and so the cost comparison, which may involve hundreds of millions of dollars or even billions of dollars, is severely distorted.
I think we should reject the arguments put forward by the shipping interests, although I must say they were most interesting and ingenious, and go back to the position of Canada prior to the Brussels meeting at which, as I have stated, we unfortunately failed to have our views accepted. It is, therefore, my purpose in moving this particular amendment to the Navigable Waters Protection Act to do precisely what should have been done last year with Bill S-23, clause 24.
As it happens, my Bill C-39 was written in 1968 before I had any knowledge of last year's government bill. Nevertheless, the way things have turned out, perhaps my bill is as valid as ever. Had Bill S-23 been passed in its entirety and not been amended by the Senate, then perhaps my bill would have become redundant. However, there are two events which have occurred since then. One was the rejection by the Senate of the clause I mentioned. The second was the failure of Canada to succeed at the International Maritime Consultative Organization meeting. Therefore, this particular amendment once more becomes one of considerable validity.
I cannot in all fairness see why we should except oil and shipping interests from the cost of pollution, an exception which makes pollution something to be borne by the public, just as the results of an act of God must be borne by the public. Pollution such as I have described results from some human action, such as somebody putting oil on a ship and somebody else having that ship go from A to B. The suggestion that if the ship is cut in two by another ship, or hits a rock through no fault of the owner, the captain or the company, then that is an act of God, the costs of which should be borne by others, is obviously absurd. Human direction has been given to put that ship where it may get into difficulty. It is only logical to assume that the people who initiate such action, the person who puts oil on board, and the shipping company should bear the cost of any subsequent cleanup. We are not dealing with small sums of money. We are dealing with enormous figures. I understand the sinking of the Torrey Canyon led to cleaning up costs of something in the neighbourhood of $12 million to $20

million. The Santa Barbara disaster off the California coast, which was not caused by a ship but by oil seepage from the seabed, led to property damages estimated at $1 billion. We are in an area in which there is tremendous cost.
I think that only by forcing all shipping lines and oil companies which transport oil by sea to take out the appropriate and necessary insurance are we ever going to make sure that we really do get around the difficulty posed by these disasters. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my hope that this particular bill will not be talked out, and that it will be possible to amend the motion so as to send it either to the committee on environmental pollution or the committee on transport, rather than to the one on health and welfare as the motion now reads.
Mr. J. M. Forresiall (Darlmoulh-Halifax
East): Mr. Speaker, once again I find myself in the peculiar position of rising to address myself to a motion moved by the hon. member and being in agreement with the principle but having a few questions at the back of my mind about the practical realities of the bill itself. I appreciate the hon. member's remarks about what seems to be the intent of government. I think the intention of the government is clear, and I think it is a step that we can not only support, but upon which we can urge the government to move more swiftly. If the hon. member's bill has that effect, then he has done a good service indeed. However, Mr. Speaker, there are some things in the bill that surprise me because the hon. member is a seafaring man.
I do not know whether his yacht is still in our delightful province, or whether he has it en route to British Columbia. However, I am tempted by the lack of his awareness, at least as indicated by what is in the bill, to say that while the hon. gentleman does have some knowledge of bathtub races and concrete boats,-he is somewhat of an expert in the latter thing-he has not addressed himself in his bill to the practical reality of ownership of a vessel or its cargo at the time of an accident to the vessel.
It must be borne in mind that accidents with vessels on the high seas, in coastal waters or in our ports are not deliberate things. They are indeed acts of God and the owners of these vessels have taken-perhaps what is no longer valid in terms of the dangers from pollution-reasonable precautions to insure and protect themselves against loss. I think all of us are aware that this has
June 9, 1970

presented the very difficult problem, in terms of pollution particularly, in the first few days of an accident of determining just exactly who does own a vessel, just exactly when a vessel is abandoned, just exactly when ownership changes from one party to another party or from first parties to second or indeed even third parties in connection with the insurance of cargo.
Many ships sailing around these days carry cargo which is worth a lot more than the ships themselves. This is one of the points the hon. gentleman was trying to make, and I agree with him. In some cases the insurance on these vessels is relatively low, and in terms of the total value of the vessel and the cargo, the greater amount is on the cargo.
This question is there, and I believe all of us on this side would have wished that the hon. member might have attempted to address himself to the problem of ownership by perhaps changing the emphasis of what he is seeking to achieve. I suggest he might have done that by seeking enabling legislation authorizing, and indeed directing, the Department of Transport or other agencies to take what action is required to immediately remove the effect of the pollution or whatever the difficulty happened to be. He could then come along and hit them, as he has quite properly done, with a provision for financial responsibility. There may be other practical reasons why such an approach cannot be made, Mr. Speaker, but it suggests what we can do within hours of the occurrence of an accident.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The explanatory notes to this bill refer to a shipping accident. They indicate that four months passed between the time of the accident and when it was finally cleaned up. In Nova Scotia, we have just experienced a disastrous accident and all Nova Scotians are aware of the sorry and dreadful state of affairs which obtains when such a disaster is not swiftly and effectively dealt with, particularly when it involves oil. The emergency should be dealt with within hours, not days or weeks. It is to this point that I think comment should be and hopefully will be directed by those who are working diligently on the preparation of a report on the Arrow disaster in Chedabucto Bay in Nova Scotia.
Speaking personally and not for my party, I believe that in cases such as the Arrow and the Torrey Canyon, where we are talking in terms of massive bulk carriers of 250,000 or

Navigable Waters Protection Act 500,000 tons-I understand that Lloyds of London in the last year or two have introduced insurance provisions for a one million ton tanker-our action immediately following an accident is vitally important. No amount of organization, laws, regulations and up to date equipment are going to prevent an accident. Mr. Speaker, when I was overtaken by the coming of private members' hour this afternoon I was saying that another principle which should govern the drafting of electoral law is that of maximizing the opportunity of electors to exercise their franchise. Although the legislation before us moves a long way in that direction, nevertheless in my opinion there remain some shortcomings within the legislation. Before I address myself to them I should like to take a moment to express my pleasure at the intent of this legislation to reduce the voting age to 18.
Three Canadian provinces now permit voting at the age of 19 and four at the age of 18. Reduction of the voting age to 18 was one of the first acts of the CCF administration when it assumed office in Saskatchewan; and it was one of the first acts passed by the legislature under the New Democratic Party government in Manitoba. Experience in at least six of these seven jurisdictions indicates that the measure has merit. I am most pleased that we at the federal level may see fit to follow suit.
To return to those areas where there would seem to be shortcomings in the attempt to maximize opportunities for the exercise of the franchise, I should like to make brief but specific reference to the problems associated with placing people on electoral lists in urban polling divisions when through some misfortune they have missed being enumerated and have also missed the court of revision procedures. This is not uncommon. I think that if the legislation is to fulfil its purpose in maximizing opportunity for electors to vote, it should take into account the fact that people can innocently miss being enumerated and miss the court of revision procedures,

June 9, 1970
Canada Elections Act
and make some provision to accommodate them.
My colleague for Regina East (Mr. Burton) has an interesting suggestion in this regard which I hope will come before the House when it is assembled in committee of the whole. The procedure that he envisages involves a person being able to swear that he is a qualified elector. His ballot, on being cast, is placed in an envelope on which his name would be found. A list of persons thus casting ballots would be supplied to each candidate in the election so that he could challenge any of the names listed. The person or persons so challenged would then be notified so they could make representations at the time the ballots were to be counted. Once this procedure had been completed, the ballots would be taken from the envelopes, put in the ballot-box so they remained completely anonymous, and then counted. This is a suggestion to which we might devote some attention in committee of the whole.
Another way to maximize opportunities to vote relates to the polling hours that are allocated. In this regard I would strongly urge the House to consider an extension of the voting hours from the seven o'clock p.m. as provided in the legislation before us to eight o'clock p.m. This would accommodate a great many industrial workers as well as people who work in white collar jobs in commerce and service industries.
Another area that we might well examine in committee of the whole with regard to maximizing voting potential concerns the number of days allocated to advance polling. There are difficulties in regard to accommodating some sectors of our population, such as the railroaders, within the two days at present allowed for advance polling. It may well be advisable to increase the number of days allotted to advance polling.
Related to the need to maximize the opportunity to vote is the necessity to minimize the opportunity for abuse of the right of voting. In this regard I am somewhat nervous about the extensive provisions for proxy voting contemplated by the bill. While such a system is obviously needed for certain groups in our community-an outstanding example of such groups being fishermen-most other groups would be equally well served, I submit, by a comprehensive system of absentee balloting. A system of absentee balloting would, I believe, be less subject to abuse than that of

proxy voting and would serve the needs of the community equally well.
A further principle which should govern the operation of election machinery in a democracy is that of unassailable impartiality on the part of electoral officials. The office of Chief Electoral Officer undoubtedly meets that standard, as does its current occupant. So, too, does the current method of redistributing seats. However, I believe that despite the irreproachable conduct of the vast majority of our returning officers, the causes of impartiality and objectivity, as well as efficiency, would be better served if these officials were appointed by the Chief Electoral Officer after the positions had been advertised and a competition had been held to fill them.
There is one further, rather small omission in the bill as it now stands which I should like to draw to the attention of the House, one which is of particular interest to those of us who represent constituencies which are partially urban and partially rural. I am referring to the difficulties involved in recognizing officially the change in character of a polling division from rural to urban and governing the operation of that poll accordingly.

Once again, one of my colleagues will have a suggestion to place before the House in this regard. As I say, he will be introducing an amendment to that effect, and I heartily recommend it to the House, assuming of course that the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) does not attempt to reduce his numerous problems by totally eliminating the posties.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Canada Elections Act, which undoubtedly ranks among the best in the world, is to allow every eligible citizen to exercise freely his right to vote.
Some time ago, a special committee was instructed to consider this legislation, and without having been closely involved in its proceedings, I have no hesitation in saying that its members have surely done a fine job, and that they deserve our consideration. All their efforts aimed at one thing, to make our act even more effective, if possible.
Many recommendations of the committee have been incorporated to the bill before the House, and I support them with a great deal of satisfaction. Other recommendations I view with less enthusiasm, while I am in total disagreement with some others. I agree with the committee that in our day and age, young people of 18 should be enfranchised and allowed to make their views known.

Until recently, we have always considered young people eligible only to the privilege of defending the country. But the maturity they have shown-and this must be admitted- entitles them to be recognized as full fledged members of our democratic society, and I am pleased to see that the committee has decided to grant them franchise.
I am also in favour of the steps taken to improve the voting procedures for the armed forces. We often have to wait several days to learn the final results of the vote in some constituencies. Needless to say that those delays result in real inconvenience, not only for the candidates themselves, but also for the population. The committee therefore deserves our gratefulness and our thanks.
I am not too very keen about the proposal which would allow vote by proxy. In my opinion, such a step would give rise to many abuses. The intent of the legislation should not be criticized, but evil-minded persons should be prevented, especially at election time, from committing abuses and even depriving certain persons of their franchise, because of the proxy vote.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Before granting proxy voting, all aspects of the matter should be considered because in each election, there are always some trouble makers who take advantage of elections to do their own little business.
The law should be as good as it can be because there will always be some ill-intentioned people to get around it. If the law enables those sad specimens of humanity to carry on their activities, I recommend that we reconsider the matter in order to fill this gap in the legislation.

The reason I set out at that time-and I think it is worth while to remind the House of it-is that the Chief Electoral Officer has made it clear that when and if the voting age is changed to 18, the electorate will be increased by about one million electors and he will only have under two years to prepare for the next federal election. On the other hand, he feels that with a better election expenses system such as that recommended by the Barbeau Commission, he could be ready in about a year's time. I think, therefore, it is obvious that prior considerations should be given to the general changes in the Elections Act.
Canada Elections Act
We have drawn up the terms of reference to establish a special committee and I expect in the next day or so a notice will be appearing in my name on the Order Paper. A number of amendments have been suggested, a useful one by the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) to include under the proxy voting system the occupation of loggers. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) added a number of other occupations to that suggestion. There are various suggestions which we would be interested in hearing in committee, so perhaps somebody will be moving an amendment not only to refer to specific categories but perhaps in more general terms to the effect that any person who by the nature of his occupation cannot attend at the advance polls or on election day in his own poll should have the privilege of proxy voting.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) made reference to a change which had some appeal to me, though I cannot say to what extent it was considered in committee. That is to give to the service electors the further anonymity of the vote to the extent it can be given by combining service electoral results and those of the advance polls. I suspect the number of votes cast by service electors may outweigh the advance polls, but it would be one step further away from identifying this group by electoral results. The House may want to consider such an amendment.
One suggestion which, subject to correction, I do not think has been widely considered by the committee and the House is that made in debate this afternoon by the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather), which I believe would find support and may have originated with the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). It is that persons incarcerated in jail or penitentiary should not be deprived of the vote. I can well understand the argument behind that proposal. If, indeed, the purpose of the incarceration is part of a rehabilitation program, then they should continue to be treated as citizens within the community. Whatever may have been the former view, perhaps the present practice should not be continued.

maintopic: SHIPPING-SAFETY STANDARDS OF FOREIGN-REGISTERED SHIPS OPERATING IN CANADIAN WATERS
SHIPPING-SAFETY STANDARDS OF FOREIGN-REGISTERED SHIPS OPERATING IN CANADIAN WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 3, I raised the following question in the House of Commons, as reported on page 7682 of Hansard:
In view of the reported statement by Dr. Mc-Taggart-Cowan that the safety standards on ships flying flags of convenience are disgraceful and that if similar standards existed with application to aircraft there would be a crash a week, I would ask the minister whether his department has laid down any regulations with respect to standards applicable to ships operating in Canadian waters, especially for those ships carrying cargoes such as oil which would cause serious environmental damage should a sinking occur?
The minister partly answered this question two days later when a similar question was asked in the House. However, I welcome this opportunity to expand on the very important principle involved, for Canada must move quickly and effectively to protect our coastal environment from the type of costly damage which we witnessed in the recent sinking of the oil tanker Arrow. Canada should insist that all shipping plying our territorial waters
7936	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion be adequately equipped for navigational purposes and conform to a high standard of safety regulations.
A few days ago Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, who heads the present task force which was set up to investigate and clean up the oil spill from the Arrow indicated that there should be an international agreement controlling the equipment and operation of oil tankers similar to the regulations which control commercial aircraft. He went on to say:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
This flags of convenience business is one of the sloppiest damn things I ever saw. If the commercial airlines ran their business like the tankers do you would be crashing a DC-8 every week and the world would say stop it.
He went on to point out that in 1944 the International Civil aviation Agreement was written, which sets out safety standards, requirements for navigation aids and control of commercial aircraft. A commercial aircraft, wherever it flies, is under its control although the essential prerogatives of the pilot are preserved in emergencies. All the nations of the world adhere to the International Civil Aviation Agreement. He felt there was no reason why countries which co-operate in the aviation field could not get together in the marine field. This is certainly a desirable objective and one which we should press for vigorously.
The flags of convenience ruling allows a vessel to operate under the shipping regulations of a country with lax rules if it flies the flag of that country. It is an easy way out for any unscrupulous owner or company to avoid those standards of safety and operation upon which their own country might insist. It allows shipping to ply international waters with dangerous cargoes whether the ship is seaworthy or not. Over the next few years we will see immense damage to the world environment unless steps are taken to remedy the situation.
I feel Canada must lay down some very strict regulations for the shipping that enters our territorial waters. Full and adequate safety standards must be insisted upon. We want no more incidents such as we witnessed in the sinking of the Arrow on the east coast.
It does not make sense to ban the drilling for oil in the Gulf of Georgia if we allow oil tankers with inadequate navigational aids, etc., into the area. The risk of another costly oil spill in our territorial waters will be greatly reduced if adequate amendments are made at an early date to the Canada Shipping Act.

DEBATES	June 9. 1970
In the international field, of course, we should press vigorously for adequate safety standards in shipping because the ecology of the oceans is also our concern.
It seems that this is the appropriate time for Canada to examine its need for a merchant marine. All the ingredients are present for a successful move into this field. We are one of the greatest importing and exporting nations in the world. We have one of the longest coastlines in the world. We have a slowly dying shipbuilding industry on both the east and west coasts. We have the skilled craftsmen and the workers to operate a shipbuilding industry. It would not only provide employment and a monetary return, but we could build into our merchant marine those safety standards required to give the best possible protection to our coastal areas. I hope this matter, together with adequate safety standards, will be high on the list of priorities at the next session of the House.

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-REQUEST FOR DEVELOPMENT OF FACILITY IN LIGHT OF POLLUTION OF LAKE ERIE
NATIONAL PARKS-REQUEST FOR DEVELOPMENT OF FACILITY IN LIGHT OF POLLUTION OF LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) the following question:
In the light of the deplorable state of Lake Erie and the need for environmental rehabilitation, and having regard to the fact that the people of Ontario are being barred from using the beaches of Lake Erie, will the minister give consideration to the development of an East Erie National Park?
I welcome this opportunity to enlarge on the urgency of this question and to hear the minister's answer. The need for action by the federal government is based on two imperatives. The first is to be in a position to clean up the pollution of Lake Erie. I quote from an article in the Canadian Churchman, which is the national publication of the Anglican Church in Canada.
It is no wonder that sometime during the last decade Lake Erie died. The largest fresh water
DEBATES	7937
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion lake in the world is now being turned slowly into a weed-choked swamp. The water near its shoreline cannot be used for cooking or drinking. Not even boiling or chlorination can remove the contamination.
The other imperative is that the urbanized industrial heartland of Ontario, with rapidly expanding population pressure, has no adequate national parks. There are no adequate recreational facilities for the public, especially for those in low-income groups who cannot afford vacations in northern cottages. Ontario has only 12 square miles of national parks, compared with Prince Edward Island which has 7.9. The matter has been fully discussed in a study by Dr. John S. Jackson of Brock University, entitled "Recreational Development and Erie East Lakeshore," in which he says that the public are restricted to narrow road allowances while vast stretches of unused beach lie on either side. He even suggested that private business interests have erected fences into the water to prevent people using their legal right of access to the beaches. My information comes from a brief presented to the federal caucus of the New Democratic Party at Hamilton, by the Association for the Preservation of Erie East Lakefront, whose initials spell APEEL.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I address an urgent appeal to the government on behalf of numerous Canadians living in the Niagara peninsula to deal with the problem in the only way available, by developing an East Erie National Park. If the minister accedes to this plea he will earn the gratitude of numerous Canadians of this and later generations who will by his action be able to enjoy an improved quality of life.

There are some problems arising from this, of course. As my hon. friend knows, this government, the government of Ontario and the municipalities concerned are taking steps to make a more direct attack on pollution than by way of establishing a national park, though I am not derogating from this very good suggestion.
One problem is the availability and very high cost of land in this particular area. I do
June 9, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion not have the sort of knowledge of the area that my hon. friend has. But as I say, the principle is good. My minister has been very active, as has the government, in the pursuit of more national parks in Canada, and he has indicated that by the year 2000 hopefully we will have a total of 80 to 100 national parks. During the last year three new national parks have been established and there are six or seven presently under negotiation with the provinces.
For example, only last Friday the minister, as part of a series of discussions extending over the last two or three months, discussed with Hon. Rene Brunelle the substantial enlargement of an existing national park in Ontario as well as the establishment of a new park. Only yesterday the minister had the agreement of the province of Quebec to the establishment of a new national park, and there is a second national park now under negotiation in that province. And so it goes across the country. I think there are seven or eight parks now under consideration.
I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood on the importance of establishing national parks in what he described as the heartland of Ontario-this applies to other provinces too-those urbanized areas where people cannot travel some distance to enjoy the facilities of a national park. The minister has held discussions in several provinces along this line and the whole matter is being pursued very actively. I thank the hon. member for bringing the matter to the attention of the House. The matter is an important one; we are conscious of it and indeed are doing a great deal about it.

maintopic: VIOLENT DISTURBANCES-MONTREAL-BOMB EXPLOSIONS-CO-OPERATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE WITH OTHER FORCES
VIOLENT DISTURBANCES-MONTREAL-BOMB EXPLOSIONS-CO-OPERATION BY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE WITH OTHER FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Canadians have the same sense of outrage that we in the House have this evening at the recent bombing activities in Westmount in the city of Montreal. This is what brings the Parliamentary Secretary and myself together for a brief exchange this evening.
It began last Friday when I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith), as minister reporting to the House for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, whether he had had an opportunity to check the serious allegations that the RCMP were not co-operating with other police forces in connection with the [Mr. Honey.)
investigation of the outrages in Montreal in the last few days.
The Solicitor General replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Immediately I saw the story published in the paper I had this matter checked into and find-
My seatmate, the hon. member for Fundy Royal (Mr. Fairweather), interrupted and asked:
Is it a canard?
The Solicitor General replied:
Yes, it is. That is precisely the point, and today's newspapers so indicate.
When the Solicitor General agreed it was a canard I believe he was ducking the question, because I think he was relying on senior officers of the RCMP who could only be expected to say that there was all the co-operation in the world. Yet, sir, a year ago, as Your Honour would well know, in the province of Quebec the Prevost Royal Commission reported about the joint workings of the police forces in that province and singled out for special observation what it regarded as the somewhat secretive work of the RCMP, who apparently set themselves apart from the other police forces there. So my first question to the Parliamentary Secretary is: What has been done to overcome the criticism voiced in the Prevost report?
I do not expect a detailed or full answer. I understand the minister's position. One cannot probe too deeply into matters of this kind. I realize that, but I think that if he could give us and the country a general reassurance it would be helpful. I have checked with members of the press gallery and others who have followed the events of that day in Westmount and in the city of Montreal. I was told the Westmount police chief was sort of tagging along while other police forces rushed on to the new bombings that occurred. He was left behind waiting for his own car to catch up with him. I think the reports of the press about the co-operation, or lack of it, in dealing with this very serious problem in the city of Montreal add to the feeling of disquiet. I am told specifically by the press-and I suppose that I either have to eat my words in this regard or prove them, and if I have an opportunity 1 feel I can do that-that there is a feeling that the lower levels of those three police forces simply do not get along.
My second question, therefore, to the Parliamentary Secretary is: What sort of thing has been done to see that all levels of these
June 9, 1970	COMMONS
police forces work together? As I have said, sir, I have spoken to people whom I regard as serious journalists, one of them being the best journalist I have worked with in 30 years in that profession, and I count on his word and on his diligence. I think it takes more than the answer that I received the other day to remove the disquiet that I have in my mind.
I should like to say in closing that I have no desire in any way, in making the speech that I do this evening, to give comfort to the people whose activities can only lead to loss of life unless they are caught-and I hope they are caught and put away for a long, long time. But I think we must have some kind of statement for the public I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will now be in a position to give one that everybody across Canada, whether they live in the metropolitan area of Montreal, in Eekum Seekum or in Vernon, B.C., will find reassuring. We hope that in future all the police forces in the Montreal area will act in harmony in dealing with a very serious national problem.
